title: The War of Words
sum: Chapter 10 begins a new tone. After nine chapters of relief and warmth, Paul turns to the people in Corinth who still doubt him, and who listen to rivals that call him weak. He quotes their charge: his letters are strong, but he is feeble in person and a poor speaker. He answers that his weapons are not those of the flesh, that he will be as bold in person as in letters if he must, and that he will not boast beyond the field God gave him.

The chapter ends with Jeremiah's rule for boasting: whoever boasts must boast in the Lord, because what counts is not what a person says about himself but what the Lord says about him. That rule shapes the long boasting that follows in chapters 11 and 12.
readings: Paul has ended the happy part of his letter (chapters 1 to 9) and now addresses the minority still siding with his rivals. The change of tone is the change of audience.

Chapters 10 to 13 were once a different letter, either written before chapters 1 to 9 (the "severe letter") or after them. The editor placed them at the end. Both views read the same words but link them to different events.

views.H: Paul writes from Macedonia, in the 50s AD, after Titus brought good news about Corinth (7:5-16). Rivals from outside had arrived in Corinth (11:4), carrying recommendations (3:1) and criticizing Paul's manner as weak. The letter goes out ahead of a third visit (12:14; 13:1).
views.C: The shift from 9:15 to 10:1 is the strongest evidence for partition. Defenders of unity note that no manuscript separates the sections and that the shift is explained by a new audience. Partition theorists (from Hausrath onward) hold that 10 to 13 is the "severe letter" of 2:3-4. Margaret Thrall (ICC) concludes that 10 to 13 is a separate letter written after chapters 1 to 8 or 9. Other commentaries set out the options without settling them.
views.L: 10:1-11 is written in the style of ancient defense speeches, with a charge quoted and answered. The key words are "boast", "measure", "flesh" and "authority", and "boast" and "weakness" will run through chapters 11 to 13. The chapter closes with a quotation that works like a motto for the next two chapters.
views.J: "Boast in the Lord" comes from Jeremiah 9:23-24, where boasting in wisdom, strength or riches is set against knowing the LORD. The "building up and tearing down" language of 10:8 echoes Jeremiah's call (Jeremiah 1:10). Paul places himself in the line of prophets whose word was despised by the people it was meant for.
views.T: Chrysostom, in his homilies on 2 Corinthians, takes the passage as a lesson in firm gentleness: Paul will not use force, but he will not give up his authority. Calvin reads the weapons of 10:4 as spiritual weapons, with doctrine among them, joined to zeal and a good conscience. Many later Protestants have used 10:5 for the battle of ideas.

deep.h: Are chapters 10 to 13 a separate letter?
deep.b:
The question has been asked since Adolf Hausrath in 1870. Reasons for a break: the tone changes sharply at 10:1; in chapter 7 Paul is full of confidence in the Corinthians (7:16), but in chapter 12 he fears what he will find when he arrives (12:20-21); and 2:3-4 and 7:8 speak of a painful letter that chapters 1 to 9 do not match. Reasons for one letter: every manuscript has the chapters in this order; the 'severe letter' of 2:3-4 was about a wrongdoer, and 10 to 13 never mention him; Paul writes of Titus's earlier visit as past (12:17-18) in a way that fits after chapter 8; and a change of subject from the loyal majority to the troublemakers is natural.

Scholars: for unity, many commentators; for partition, Hausrath (who identified 10 to 13 with the severe letter) and Thrall (who sees a separate letter written later). The Plain English and the notes here read the text as it stands, whichever view is right.

echoes: Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 9:23-24; 1 Corinthians 1:31; 1 Corinthians 2:1-5; 1 Corinthians 4:21; Galatians 2:7-9; Romans 15:19-24; Ephesians 6:10-17; Philippians 2:8

settings.what: Paul's answer to the charge that he is bold only from a distance
settings.to: The church at Corinth, especially the part that doubted him and listened to rivals; the loyal majority hears it read aloud beside them
settings.when: From Macedonia, in the 50s AD, before Paul's third visit
settings.why: To warn the doubters that his letters and his presence are the same, and that he will use his authority, but only to build. The hard words are a last appeal before he comes, so that when he arrives there is nobody left to punish.
settings.readers: A church of mostly Gentiles, a few Jews, some wealthy and many poor, divided between loyal and critical members, who had heard the rivals say his speech and looks were unimpressive.
views: The tone changes because Paul turns from the loyal majority to a minority.
These chapters are the "severe letter" of 2:3-4, sent before chapters 1 to 9.
New trouble reached Paul after chapter 9, and he wrote again (Thrall: a separate letter after chapters 1 to 9, not the severe letter).

settings.what: Paul's reply on boasting and the limits of his field
settings.to: The church at Corinth, with the rivals who had come into the church in mind
settings.when: The same letter, written from Macedonia
settings.why: To say that he does not rate himself by his own measure, nor take credit for others' work, and that the only recommendation that counts is the Lord's. It also sets up his hope that Corinth will become a base for a mission further west.
settings.readers: A church whose sense of worth depended on the status of its teachers, and which was proud of having the best.

title: The Fool's Boast
sum: Paul opens with a picture of jealousy: he promised the Corinthians to one husband, Christ, and fears that they, like Eve, will be fooled by the serpent. He names the danger as rivals who preach "another Jesus", whom he calls false apostles and servants of Satan in disguise. Then he does what he did not want to do: he says that if they put up with fools, they can put up with him, and he boasts.

But his boast is a parody. He lists his Jewish pedigree in three short lines, then a long catalog of beatings, shipwrecks, dangers and hunger, and ends with a story of running away in a basket. He boasts only of weakness. The chapter is the heart of what is sometimes called the 'fool's speech'.
readings: Paul adopts the style of a boaster to show how foolish boasting is. Every claim is turned upside down: instead of honors, he lists scars. This is the most common modern reading.
The list also proves something plain: no one in Corinth had suffered for the gospel as much as Paul. He was claiming the credentials of a real apostle. Both can be true at once.

views.H: Corinth prized rhetoric, patronage and public status. Paul had refused Corinthian money (11:7-9), which the Corinthians took as a sign he was not a serious teacher. The rivals carried credentials and probably took pay (11:20). Paul's list of sufferings can be set beside Acts, which reports only a few of them. His flight from Damascus under King Aretas points to a date between AD 37 and Aretas's death about AD 40, if Aretas then ruled the city.
views.C: Who the 'super-apostles' (11:5) and the 'false apostles' (11:13) were is the main critical problem of the letter. Views: two groups, the Jerusalem apostles and their agents (argued by some scholars); one group, the same intruders named ironically (many recent commentators); and, for who the intruders were, Jews shaped by Hellenistic ideas (Georgi) or Judaizing Jewish Christians.
views.L: The speech is a 'periautologia', self-praise made acceptable by irony. Paul uses 'fool' (a word for someone lacking sense) again and again in this and the next chapter. The suffering catalog (11:23-29) is a literary kind found in Stoic writing; he fits his own hardships into it and turns it into a boast of weakness. The final story, the descent in a basket, is the punch line.
views.J: The three questions of 11:22 are the credentials of a Jew of the day. Paul's lashes (11:24) came from Jewish authorities, and the thirty-nine blows follow Deuteronomy 25:3 and Jewish custom. His claim to be 'Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham' is a claim to be a Jew among Jews, not an ex-Jew. Eve and the serpent (11:3) were read in several Jewish ways, one linking the serpent to sexual deception.
views.T: Chrysostom stresses that Paul boasts only under compulsion and for the Corinthians' good. Calvin reads 11:3-4 as a warning that the church's purity lies in simple fidelity to Christ's word. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teachers alike have applied 11:13-15 to false teachers who look like angels of light.

deep.b:
The Greek hyperlian apostoloi (11:5; 12:11) is sarcastic: hyperlian means "beyond the limit", and the Plain's "super-apostles" is a label that tries to keep the mockery. Pseudapostoloi (11:13) is Paul's invention. Whether they are the same people is the question.

Same group, intruders: many recent commentators think both phrases describe the newcomers: Jewish Christians who arrived in Corinth with letters of recommendation, claimed Christ, claimed apostleship, boasted of visions and signs, charged fees and, by Paul's account, ruled the church harshly (11:20).

Two groups: Some scholars have thought the 'super-apostles' were the Jerusalem apostles themselves and the 'false apostles' were the intruders who used their names. For this: 11:5 and 11:13 use two different labels, and Galatians 2:6 is itself guarded about 'those who seemed to be something'. Against it: Paul agreed with the Jerusalem apostles on the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:11; Galatians 2:9), and the harsh words about Satan's servants in 11:13-15 are said of the 'false apostles', which would be a hard thing to say of Peter.

What they taught: Paul says 'another Jesus' (11:4) but never lists their doctrine. Proposals include law-keeping Jewish Christians like those at Galatia, Jews shaped by Hellenistic ideas (Georgi), gnostics, and spiritual enthusiasts boasting of visions. Jerry Sumney argues that the letter itself must be the main source for any portrait, with outside reconstructions given limited weight. The arguments below (11:22: 'Hebrews', 'Israelites') make a Jewish-Christian background likely.

deep.h: The suffering list set beside Acts
deep.b:
Paul's tally by the time of this letter (in the 50s AD): five synagogue lashings (not in Acts), three beatings with rods (one in Acts, at Philippi), one stoning (Lystra), three shipwrecks (none in Acts before Acts 27), a night and a day at sea, many journeys, many dangers, and imprisonments (Acts shows one, Philippi). This shows that Acts is selective rather than complete. It tells us about Paul's work, but it does not tell everything that happened to him.

1 Clement 5:6 says Paul was thrown into captivity seven times, a count that agrees with the idea that the full list is longer than Acts reports.

echoes: Genesis 3:1-13; Deuteronomy 25:1-3; Philippians 3:4-8; Acts 9:23-25; Acts 14:19; Acts 16:22-24; 1 Corinthians 4:9-13; 1 Corinthians 9:1-18; Galatians 1:6-9; Revelation 2:2; Didache 11:3-6

settings.what: Paul's jealousy for the church and his warning about false apostles
settings.to: The church at Corinth, including those drawn to the visiting teachers
settings.when: The same letter, as the opening of the 'fool's speech'
settings.why: To make them see that listening to a 'different Jesus' is not a harmless courtesy but unfaithfulness to the one they were engaged to. He also explains why he took no pay from them, and names the rivals as disguised servants of Satan so that they cannot be taken at face value.
settings.readers: A church that admired strong, polished teachers and that had accepted the newcomers' claims.
views: The rivals preached a really different Jesus or gospel (law-keeping, or a power-and-glory Jesus without the cross).
The difference was in manner and authority, and Paul's strong words are hyperbole about a quarrel over status.

settings.what: The fool's speech: Paul's boasting in weakness
settings.to: The church at Corinth, including the part that admired the visiting teachers' boasting
settings.when: In the same letter, as its high point; Paul says he is forced to it (12:11)
settings.why: To beat the rivals at their own game and show how little it proves. He lists what a real apostle suffers, gives one great experience (12:1-4) and then says it is the weakness, not the vision, that proves him. The point for the hearers: the one who looks weak may be the true apostle.
settings.readers: Corinthian hearers who knew the rules of a boasting contest and would have enjoyed the reversal.
views: Paul mocks boasting by boasting badly.
Paul also seriously sets out his claim to be an apostle, using the rivals' own categories.

title: Strength in Weakness
sum: Paul now gives the one thing he could boast about, an ascent to the third heaven, fourteen years before. He tells it of 'a man in Christ' and gives no details, then says he will not boast of it. He moves at once to the thorn in the flesh, a painful gift that came with the visions and that he begged the Lord three times to remove. The answer was no, with a promise: 'My grace is enough for you. Power is made complete in weakness.'

The rest of the chapter returns to the practical quarrel. Paul says he was no burden to the Corinthians, defends Titus and the collection, and tells them he fears what he will find when he arrives for the third time.
readings: Paul really was taken up, perhaps in the body, perhaps not, and heard words he may not repeat. He gives the story to answer the rivals' boasts of visions (12:1), but refuses to base his authority on it.
A story told at a distance on purpose
The third-person style, the lack of detail and the quick turn to the thorn show that Paul wants to say that visions are not the test. His authority rests on weakness, as in Christ.

views.H: About fourteen years before the letter, in the early AD 40s, Paul was in Syria and Cilicia, a time Acts barely describes. The collection for Jerusalem, handled by Titus (8:6, 16-24), became the basis for a charge of fraud (12:16-18). The 'third visit' (12:14) follows the 'painful visit' of 2:1.
views.C: The man is Paul (almost all scholars), though a few read him as Paul's 'other self'. The thorn has been identified as illness (malaria: Ramsay; eye disease; migraine; epilepsy), as human opponents, as temptation or spiritual struggle, or as grief; the text does not say. The variants at 12:1, 12:7 and 12:9 mark places where the Byzantine text smooths a hard Greek sentence.
views.L: 12:1-10 is the center of the fool's speech and has its own shape: vision (1-4), refusal to boast (5-6), thorn (7), prayer (8), answer (9a), paradox (9b-10). The repeated 'so that I would not lift myself too high' (twice in 12:7) and 'weakness' (five times in 12:5-10) mark the theme. The 'threes' of 12:2, 8, 14 and 13:1 link the chapter to the next.
views.J: The ascent to a heavenly 'Paradise' belongs to the same world as Jewish apocalypses and later mystical texts (2 Enoch 8; Hagigah 14b), as a comparison only. The 'thorn' language belongs to the Septuagint's picture of hostile neighbors (Numbers 33:55; Ezekiel 28:24). The Lord's answer to a lament recalls the oracles of salvation in the Psalms.
views.T: Chrysostom thought the thorn was human opponents (Alexander the coppersmith and others), not an illness. Augustine used 12:2-4 to build his theory of three kinds of vision (Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 12), and Aquinas held that in his rapture Paul saw the divine essence (Summa II-II q.175). Calvin read the thorn as temptation of every kind, and Luther's 'theologian of the cross' (Heidelberg Disputation, 1518) fits the pattern of 12:9-10. Gregory Palamas tied Paul's rapture to the uncreated light. See the cards.

deep.b:
Paul does not say. The main answers:

1. A physical illness. Candidates include an eye problem (suggested by Galatians 4:13-15, 'you would have dug out your own eyes and given them to me'), malaria (William Ramsay), migraine, epilepsy, or a speech problem (compare 10:10). Against: Paul's word is 'messenger of Satan', and the Septuagint uses the word 'thorn' for human enemies.

2. Human opponents. Chrysostom and many later readers took the 'messenger' as a person or persons who opposed Paul. The Septuagint's 'thorns in the eyes' (Numbers 33:55) are people. Against: the thorn is said to be 'in the flesh' and to have followed the visions.

3. Temptation or spiritual struggle. The Latin Vulgate has 'a stimulus of the flesh', so many medieval writers read it as fleshly temptation. Calvin read it as spiritual trial in general. Against: Paul says nothing of sin here.

4. Emotional or spiritual distress. Some modern writers think of depression, anxiety, guilt over his early persecution of the church, or grief over Israel.

5. A demonic attack. The 'messenger of Satan' is a demon who strikes him again and again, with God's permission, as in Job.

Most scholars say the vagueness is part of the point. Because the thorn is unnamed, readers in every age can see their own pain in it. The Lord's answer is the same whatever it was.

Paul speaks of the 'third heaven' and 'Paradise' as one place, with no explanation, so he expects the Corinthians to know the idea. In the ancient Jewish world there was a belief in several heavens (three, five, seven or ten, in various texts). 2 Enoch 8 puts Paradise in the third heaven; the Life of Adam and Eve puts Paradise there too (Apocalypse of Moses 37:4-5). Later rabbinic tradition tells of four sages who 'entered Paradise' (Hagigah 14b), and still later mystical texts describe journeys through the heavenly palaces. These are comparisons, many of them later than Paul. Alan Segal and C. R. A. Morray-Jones have argued that Paul belongs to a Jewish mystical tradition; others warn that Paul says too little to be sure.

Paul's own attitude is guarded. He does not tell what he saw, he says he does not know if it was in the body, and he refuses to build his authority on it. The Corinthians, who valued spiritual experiences (1 Corinthians 12 to 14), would have been surprised.
deep.refs: 2 Enoch 8; Apocalypse of Moses 37:5; Hagigah 14b; Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7

deep.title: A thread of threes in 12:2 to 13:1
deep.b: Claude's observation, offered with caution: threes run through this stretch: the third heaven (12:2), the three prayers (12:8), the third visit (12:14; 13:1) and 'two or three witnesses' (13:1). The first three are almost certainly just what happened or what Paul planned. But the last may shape how the earlier ones are told. The Deuteronomy rule needs two or three witnesses; Paul may be shaping his story so that his own three prayers and the Lord's reply count as testimony that his weakness is God's will. No commentator I know builds an argument on this; it may only be a coincidence of numbers.

echoes: Numbers 33:55; Ezekiel 28:24; Job 1:12; Job 2:6; Exodus 40:34-35; Mark 14:32-42; Luke 23:43; John 1:14; Galatians 1:12; Galatians 2:2; Galatians 4:13-15; 1 Corinthians 4:14-15; 1 Corinthians 5:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:17; Revelation 2:7

settings.by: Paul, writing of "a man in Christ"
settings.to: The church at Corinth, who valued visions and spiritual experiences and heard the rivals boast of them
settings.when: Told in the 50s AD about something that happened about fourteen years earlier
settings.why: To show that Paul has more of such experiences than anyone, and that he will not make them the basis of his claim. It also keeps hearers from placing him higher than they can see in him.
settings.readers: Hearers who had enjoyed tongues and visions (1 Corinthians 12 to 14).
views: The man is Paul, written in the third person so he does not praise himself.
A few read him as another person or as Paul's ecstatic self, kept apart from his daily self.

settings.what: The thorn and the Lord's answer
settings.to: The church at Corinth; the Lord's words were first said to Paul alone in prayer
settings.when: The thorn came after the vision about fourteen years earlier; the answer came after three prayers, and Paul reports it now in the 50s AD
settings.why: To tell a church that expects a leader to be strong and healthy that his weakness is the place where Christ's power can be seen. The Lord's answer, 'My grace is enough for you', is the key line of the letter.
settings.readers: A church where strength meant status, patronage and eloquence.
views: The thorn story is part of the answer to those who ask for signs and strength.
It also stands as a general lesson for anyone in suffering that is not removed.

settings.what: Paul's appeal: no burden, Titus, and his fears for his visit
settings.when: The end of the letter's main argument, before the third visit
settings.why: To answer the charge that he gained from them by trickery (through Titus and the collection), to remind them of the signs he did among them, and to say that all he does is to build them up. He ends by naming what he fears to find: quarrels and old, unrepented sins.
settings.readers: A church where some had said Paul was dishonest with money.

traditions.q: Does God sometimes refuse to heal, as with Paul's thorn?
views: Christ healed, and the Church prays for the sick in the Anointing of the Sick, but a sick person united to Christ's passion shares in his saving suffering; the Church does not promise physical healing in every case (Catechism 1499-1532).
Chrysostom read Paul's thorn as human opponents, not an illness, and taught that God uses trials to keep us humble (Homilies on 2 Corinthians).

In the Heidelberg Disputation (1518, thesis 21) Luther sets the theologian of glory against the theologian of the cross, who calls a thing what it actually is. Lutherans read Paul's 'power is made complete in weakness' in that light, but the Disputation itself does not discuss the thorn.

Calvin took the thorn to mean temptation of every kind, through which the Lord keeps believers humble. The Westminster Confession teaches that God sometimes leaves his own children for a season to manifold temptations (5.5).
The Assemblies of God teaches that divine healing is provided for in the atonement and is for believers today (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 12). That statement does not address the thorn.

traditions.q: What did Paul see in the third heaven?
views: Aquinas, following Augustine, taught that Paul in his rapture saw God's essence itself (Augustine, Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 12; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 175, a. 3). Not all Catholic scholars follow them.

Gregory Palamas tied Paul's rapture to the uncreated light, a light of revelation beyond every creature (Triads). Orthodox teaching on the essence-energies distinction holds that God's essence "cannot be comprehended in words," while his energies "enable us to experience something of the Divine" (the page that states this does not mention Paul's rapture).
Calvin warned against curiosity about what Paul saw and heard, and said we should seek only the knowledge we need and leave the rest to God.

traditions.q: Do the signs of an apostle still happen?
views: Many Reformed teachers hold that miracles and the apostles' office ended with the apostolic age, as signs for the Church's founding (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, 1918). Not every Reformed church holds this.

Pentecostal churches such as the Assemblies of God teach that divine healing, provided for in the atonement, is for believers today (Statement of Fundamental Truths, 12). On apostles, the Assemblies of God holds that the church "maintains an apostolic function without needing apostolic offices or titles," and that missions and church planting "are more uniquely representative of the apostolic function."
The Orthodox Church holds that its bishops come down in direct descent from the apostles (Orthodox Church in America, The Orthodox Faith, vol. 3).

The Twelve and Paul were founders and have no equals, but their authority is handed on by bishops (Catechism 77, 861-862). Miracles continue, and the Church recognizes them in the lives of the saints as signs of credibility, not as proofs required for faith (Catechism 156, 799-801 on charisms).

title: Test Yourselves
sum: Paul ends with a warning and a blessing. He is coming a third time, and this time he will hear charges on the word of two or three witnesses and will not spare anyone who has not changed. The Corinthians have asked for proof that Christ speaks in him. He answers: Christ was crucified in weakness and lives by God's power, and Paul is the same. Then he turns the demand back: examine yourselves, to see if Christ is in you.

The last verses are brief and warm: be glad, be restored, take comfort, agree, live in peace; greet one another with a holy kiss; and the blessing of the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.
readings: The chapter ends the letter's quarrel with a threat: if the church does not change, Paul will use his authority in person, and he will be hard.
The warning is meant to make the visit unnecessary. Paul says that he hopes to build up and not tear down (13:10), and the closing is a prayer for restoration.

views.H: This is the end of a letter written from Macedonia in the 50s AD. Paul's third visit to Corinth came soon after: Acts 20:2-3 puts him in Greece for three months, and he wrote Romans from there. The 'holy kiss' and the greetings of 'the saints' (probably the Macedonian churches) were customary closings.
views.C: 13:10 returns to the wording of 10:8 (authority for building up, not tearing down), a link that defenders of unity point to. The numbering of the last verses differs in Greek and English. The Byzantine text and Textus Receptus add 'Amen' and a note that the letter was written from Philippi by Titus and Luke; the critical editions omit it.
views.L: The 'test' words (proof, test, pass, fail) run through 13:3-7 and tie back to 10:18. 13:4 is a parallel: Christ's weakness and life, then Paul's own. The closing is a miniature of the whole: joy, restoration, comfort, agreement and peace are the opposite of the vices of 12:20.
views.J: 'Two or three witnesses' comes from Deuteronomy 19:15 and 17:6; it was the rule of Jewish courts for any charge. The holy kiss follows Jewish and Greek greeting customs. The blessing sounds like the Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 in form, a prayer for good on a whole community, though no verbal link is clear.
views.T: The blessing is one of the greetings that open the Roman Catholic Mass (Order of Mass); it is one of the places where Paul names the Lord Jesus, God and the Spirit together.

deep.b:
13:14 is the only place in Paul's letters where the Lord Jesus Christ, God and the Holy Spirit stand together in a prayer. The order is Christ, God, Spirit, and each is paired with a gift: grace, love, fellowship. It is not a doctrine of the Trinity, but it shows that Paul and his readers already spoke of the three together in worship. A comparable list appears in 1 Corinthians 12:4-6 and 2 Corinthians 1:21-22, and later in Matthew 28:19.

The Nicene churches have read it as an early sign of what the creeds later spelled out. Critical scholars add that the language here is about experience and worship, not about the inner life of God. Both readings can be held together. For how the churches differ, see the card.

In 13:5 Paul reverses the Corinthians' request for proof. The test is 'whether you are in the faith', and the proof of Christ in Paul is the church he founded (compare 3:2-3; 1 Corinthians 9:2). Churches have also used the verse to teach that a believer should check that his faith is real. That reading is old in the church. For how the traditions use it for assurance, see the card.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15; Numbers 6:24-26; Matthew 18:16; Matthew 28:19; John 8:17; 1 Corinthians 4:21; 1 Corinthians 5:5; 1 Corinthians 11:28; 1 Corinthians 12:4-6; 1 Corinthians 16:20; Philippians 2:6-11; Romans 16:16; Acts 20:2-3

settings.what: The warning of a third visit and the call to self-test
settings.to: The church at Corinth, above all those who had sinned before and not repented, and those who asked for proof that Christ speaks in him
settings.when: At the close of the letter, shortly before Paul's third visit (Acts 20:2-3)
settings.why: To give a last warning so that the visit will not be a trial: he promises fairness (two or three witnesses) and no leniency toward the unrepentant. He asks them to test themselves and gives the reason for the letter: to avoid having to be harsh, since his authority is for building up.
settings.readers: A church that had asked for proof of his apostleship and was divided over him.

settings.to: The church at Corinth, with greetings from the saints with Paul
settings.when: The end of the letter, read aloud when the church gathered
settings.why: To leave them with a short list of what a restored church looks like, a kiss as a sign of reconciliation, and the blessing of the Lord Jesus, God and the Spirit. Letters were read aloud in the assembly, so the blessing would be heard as a prayer.
settings.readers: A church to which the whole letter, with its hard parts, would first be read in one sitting.

traditions.q: Can a believer be sure that he is "in the faith"?
views: No one can know with the certainty of faith that he has received God's grace; Trent also condemns claiming an absolute, infallible certainty of final perseverance (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 9 and canons 13-16).

Faith, which believes that sins are forgiven for Christ's sake, comes through the Word and the sacraments (Augsburg Confession, Articles V and XII); the Confession also condemns those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Spirit (Article XII).
Orthodox writers describe salvation as a life-long process of being saved, not a finished status, and say a baptized believer can fall away (Orthodox Church in America, questions on Hebrews 6:4-6).

True believers can be certain of salvation, and 13:5 is read as a call to self-examination; the Westminster Confession (ch. 18) says this infallible assurance is not of the essence of faith, and a believer may wait long and struggle to reach it.
Wesley taught the 'direct witness of the Spirit' and also the 'witness of our own spirit': a believer knows by the Spirit's inner testimony that he is a child of God (Sermons 10, 11 and 12).
The 1689 Confession (ch. 18) teaches that true believers can have an infallible assurance, founded on the truth of God's promises, though a true believer may wait long for it.

traditions.q: Does the blessing of 13:14 teach the Trinity?
views: The Catechism teaches the Trinity at 232-267, beginning from the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19 (232); that section is not a commentary on 13:14. The blessing is one of the greetings that open the Mass (Order of Mass, Introductory Rites).
The Orthodox Church confesses one God in three persons in the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381).
Reformed confessions teach one God in three persons (Westminster Confession 2.3, 'three Persons of one substance, power, and eternity').
The three are not three persons but one God known in three roles or manifestations, and all fullness is in Jesus; 13:14 names the one God by three of his works.

Unitarian and Socinian teachers do not read the blessing as a statement of three persons in one being (the Racovian Catechism, 1605, denies Christ's personal pre-existence); on this view it is a worship formula naming God, the Lord Jesus Christ and the Spirit.
